drills.q: A GET request is slow. Show the curl command you'd run and how you'd read the output to find out why.
drills.a: curl -w "@curl-format.txt" -o /dev/null -s <url>, reading the deltas: time_connect - time_namelookup = DNS, time_appconnect - time_connect = TLS, time_starttransfer - time_appconnect = server processing (usual culprit), time_total - time_starttransfer = body transfer.

drills.q: Walk through reading curl -v output line by line.
drills.a: * lines are connection/TLS metadata (DNS, TCP connect, negotiated TLS version/cipher, ALPN, cert chain) from curl itself. > lines are the literal bytes curl sent -- verify your intended headers actually went out. < lines are the literal response headers from the server -- ground truth that can catch a proxy silently rewriting something in between.

drills.q: The DNS lookup phase in your -w timing breakdown is slow. What do you check next?
drills.a: Try --resolve to bypass DNS and hit the known IP directly, confirming the rest of the timing is normal -- isolates resolver latency from a genuinely slow/misconfigured upstream DNS server, and check whether the client is caching resolutions at all.

drills.q: Why doesn't your POST body survive a redirect, and how do you force it to?
drills.a: curl converts POST to GET and drops the body by default on 301/302, matching browser convention; only 307/308 explicitly preserve method and body. Force with explicit -X POST, but be deliberate -- this overrides the server's semantic hint and can break a flow that intentionally wanted GET-after-redirect.

drills.q: Your JSON POST fails with a parse error server-side even though the JSON is valid. Diagnose, and explain -d vs --data-raw.
drills.a: -d/--data defaults Content-Type to application/x-www-form-urlencoded; the server's JSON deserializer is choking on a form-encoded parse. Fix: explicit -H "Content-Type: application/json". -d interprets a leading @ as 'read from file'; --data-raw sends the literal string even if it starts with @.

drills.q: How do you debug a TLS handshake failure with curl, and does -k fix it?
drills.a: curl -v and read the certificate block: 'unable to get local issuer certificate' = missing intermediate/untrusted private CA (fix with --cacert); 'certificate has expired' is literal; hostname mismatch shows subject/SAN not matching the requested host. -k doesn't fix anything -- it just stops checking, confirming the app layer works past the handshake but leaving the trust-chain problem in place for every real client that validates properly.

drills.q: --connect-timeout 3 -m 10 is set but a request still hangs 30s. What's wrong?
drills.a: Either the timeout wasn't actually applied (common when curl is wrapped by another tool/library with its own timeout config overriding or ignoring the CLI flag), or DNS resolution hung before either timer started in some resolver/curl combinations. Verify --connect-timeout is guarding the connect phase and -m is guarding the whole request; check the wrapping layer's own timeout handling.

drills.q: How do you hit one specific backend behind a load balancer without SSH access to it, and what's the difference between the two flags that do this?
drills.a: --resolve api.example.com:443:<ip> or --connect-to api.example.com:443:<ip>:443. --resolve fully overrides DNS resolution for that host. --connect-to only redirects the TCP connection target while keeping Host header, SNI, and cert validation against the original hostname -- useful when you want cert checks to still validate against the real name.

drills.q: A -k flag snuck into a shipped production health-check script. What's wrong with it, and how do you catch this in CI?
drills.a: -k disables cert verification entirely, so the health check reports 'healthy' even with an expired cert, wrong hostname, or active MITM -- exactly the failures TLS exists to catch. Catch it by grepping/linting CI for -k or --insecure in any committed shell script and failing the build on a match.

drills.q: Should you add --retry to a script calling a payment API? Justify.
drills.a: Not without checking idempotency first. --retry only retries transient transport failures and select response codes -- it has no concept of your endpoint's idempotency semantics. Retrying a non-idempotent POST risks a duplicate side effect (double charge); the decision to retry belongs with the caller's understanding of the operation, not the flag.

drills.q: A -F multipart upload works for a 1KB file but chokes on a 2GB file. Where's the likely bottleneck?
drills.a: Likely the server's max body size / multipart buffer limit, or a client library's in-memory buffering of the multipart body rather than streaming. curl itself streams from disk with @filename, so check server/proxy limits first, not curl's own behavior.

drills.q: Design a curl-based synthetic check for a critical external dependency, and name its blind spot.
drills.a: curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_starttransfer} %{time_total}\n" --connect-timeout 3 -m 10 <url>, on a schedule, piping write-out fields into metrics, alerting on non-2xx or time_starttransfer exceeding an SLO. Blind spot: it only observes network conditions from one vantage point/region; a regional DNS or network issue elsewhere won't show up -- needs multi-region checks or explicit acknowledgment it's a coarse first-line signal, not a replacement for real APM.
